thoughts.text: You have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
thoughts.act: Name one thing today that is not yours to control, and let it go.

thoughts.text: Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one.
thoughts.act: Do one small thing today you would admire in someone else.

thoughts.text: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste much of it.
thoughts.act: Find one hour you will give away today, and take it back.

lessons.title: The ledger: what you count, you can change
lessons.body:
**The idea.** Benjamin Franklin picked thirteen virtues and kept a small book with a column for each day. Each evening he marked where he had slipped. He did not try to fix everything at once: he took one virtue a week and let the others rest.

**First principles.** A habit is a loop of a cue, a move and a result. Most of the time the result is invisible, so the loop never closes. A count makes it visible. Seeing a slip written down is cheaper than the slip itself, and it asks for no willpower, only honesty.

**An example.** Franklin wanted order. By his own account he never reached it, yet he called himself a better and happier man for trying. The ledger was the point, not the score.

**One move for today.** Pick one thing you want to do less of or more of. Draw a line on paper. Tonight, make one mark per time it happened. Do not judge the number. Tomorrow, look at it again.
lessons.summary: Count one habit for a day so the loop closes; one virtue a week.

lessons.title: Inversion: ask how it fails
lessons.body:
**The idea.** The mathematician Jacobi said to invert, always invert. Charlie Munger made it a daily tool: instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, and avoid that.

**First principles.** Some goals are fuzzy, while their opposites are sharp. It is hard to say what a great day looks like, but easy to list what ruins one. Removing the ruinous things often gets most of the way there, and it is a smaller task than inventing the perfect plan.

**An example.** Seneca asks us to imagine losing what we have: a friend, our health, our home. Seen from the other side, what remains looks like a gift, and we treat it that way.

**One move for today.** Write the goal you care about this week. Under it, list three ways to make it fail for certain. Cross out the one you are quietly doing already.
lessons.summary: List what would guarantee failure and remove it.
